about: What the tap panel says about a tapped part of a big (PDB) molecule: friendly chain names (names, with the file's own _entity.pdbx_description kept in entities), part lines saying what that part does in this protein (lines), and the small parts each file holds (holds, for the card's note on balls and ribbons). Keyed by molecule id. A line's at picks what it covers: het (a small part by its CCD code), seq (author-numbered ranges, in chains or every chain), res ([chain, number] pairs), comp (every residue of that code in chains) or chains (a whole chain). up lines a range up with UniProt (file number = UniProt position + offset) and tools/build_parts.py checks every residue against the saved UniProt sequence. {chain} in a sentence is filled with the friendly chain name. Every sentence names its sources (s). UI words live in molecules.json ui (pick.*, holds.*). Generated keys (entities, chains, holds, copied sources) come from python tools/build_parts.py, which also checks the file. No em or en dashes.

motm-1.cite: PDB-101 Molecule of the Month: Myoglobin (January 2000).
motm-1.checked: 2026-10-01: small, bright red protein, common in muscle cells, gives meat much of its red colour; stores oxygen for when muscles work hard; John Kendrew and coworkers determined its structure; first protein to have its atomic structure determined.

motm-11.cite: PDB-101 Molecule of the Month: Rubisco (November 2000).
motm-11.checked: 2026-10-01: attaches carbon dioxide to ribulose bisphosphate, a five-carbon sugar; most plentiful single enzyme on Earth; fixes only about three carbon dioxide molecules per second; plant form has eight large and eight small chains; 8ruc named.

motm-12.cite: PDB-101 Molecule of the Month: Pepsin (December 2000).
motm-12.checked: 2026-10-01: digests proteins in strong stomach acid; protein chains bind in its deep active-site groove and are broken into smaller pieces; works best in strong hydrochloric acid; made with an extra 44 amino acids that block the groove and are clipped off in the stomach.

motm-147.cite: PDB-101 Molecule of the Month: Rhodopsin (March 2012).
motm-147.checked: 2026-10-01: the molecule that senses light; retinal absorbs a photon and one bond flips from bent (cis) to extended (trans); rod cells can be triggered by a single photon; launches a G-protein signal leading to a nerve signal to the brain; 1f88 shown.

motm-38.cite: PDB-101 Molecule of the Month: Potassium Channels (February 2003).
motm-38.checked: 2026-10-01: allow potassium to flow across the membrane while blocking other ions; one sodium ion passes for every ten thousand potassium ions; four identical proteins forming a pore down the centre; nerve cells concentrate potassium inside and pump sodium out before a signal; bacterial channel from entry 1bl8.

motm-54.cite: PDB-101 Molecule of the Month: Acetylcholinesterase (June 2004).
motm-54.checked: 2026-10-01: breaks acetylcholine into acetic acid and choline, stopping the signal; each in about 80 microseconds; active site in a deep pocket; partial blocking drugs raise neurotransmitter levels (Alzheimer's); first studied in electric fish such as the torpedo ray; 1acj shown.

motm-6.cite: PDB-101 Molecule of the Month: HIV-1 Protease (June 2000).
motm-6.checked: 2026-10-01: cuts the long polyprotein into protein-sized pieces; two identical chains of 99 amino acids; a tunnel covered by two flexible flaps; drugs mimic a protein chain but cannot be cleaved; ritonavir shown with entry 1hxw.

motm-62.cite: PDB-101 Molecule of the Month: Major Histocompatibility Complex (February 2005).
motm-62.checked: 2026-10-01: class I MHC on the surface of most cells protects from viral infection; cells display pieces of old proteins on their surfaces; each person has their own MHC types and grafts with different types trigger the immune system; human MHC called HLA; 1hsa named.

motm-64.cite: PDB-101 Molecule of the Month: Kinesin (April 2005).
motm-64.checked: 2026-10-01: carries cargo along microtubules, crawling hand over hand; cells built three types of ATP-powered motors; kinesin in entry 3kin is two chains with two motor domains holding ADP.

motm-7.cite: PDB-101 Molecule of the Month: Nucleosome (July 2000).
motm-7.checked: 2026-10-01: eight histone proteins bundled together, encircled by two loops of DNA; nucleosomes protect DNA strands from physical damage; intact nucleosome in entry 1aoi.

motm-actin.title: Molecule of the Month: Actin
motm-actin.checked: Actin filaments form the cytoskeleton and the ladder myosin climbs; up to 5 percent of the protein in a typical cell; each actin holds an ATP, broken to ADP after joining a filament, ADP actin lets go more easily; treadmilling; phalloidin from the death cap mushroom clogs cells with actin filaments; crystal structures hold a single actin, not a filament; actin is U-shaped with the nucleotide deep in the groove between the two arms.

motm-aquaporin.title: Molecule of the Month: Aquaporin
motm-aquaporin.checked: Membranes resist water; kidneys and the eye use aquaporins to control water flow; four identical chains, each with its own channel; water passes single file; the red blood cell aquaporin; two asparagines hold a central water in a set orientation so the channel cannot pass protons; constriction controls what passes; mercury blocks water flow in red blood cells; blockers studied for glaucoma.

motm-atp-synthase.title: Molecule of the Month: ATP Synthase
motm-atp-synthase.checked: Builds most of the ATP in cells; two rotary motors, F0 in the membrane powered by hydrogen ions and F1 the chemical motor; F0 turns the rotor and axle and F1 becomes a generator making ATP; the axle forces F1 through three shapes: bind ADP and phosphate, make the bond, release ATP; the structure is solved in parts.
motm-atp-synthase.cite: Molecule of the Month: ATP Synthase

motm-collagen.title: Molecule of the Month: Collagen
motm-collagen.checked: About one quarter of the protein in the body; strengthens tendons and supports skin and organs; bones and teeth add mineral to collagen; three chains in a triple helix; every third amino acid is glycine, which fits inside the helix; proline and hydroxyproline fill many other positions; hydroxyproline needs vitamin C, lack of it causes scurvy; each chain is over 1400 amino acids long; in 1cag an alanine replaces a glycine and crowds the neighbouring chains; heated collagen becomes gelatin.

motm-dna.title: Molecule of the Month: DNA
motm-dna.checked: Each cell carries about 1.5 gigabytes of genetic information; strands pair into the double helix; A pairs with T, G with C through hydrogen bonds; major and minor grooves expose chemical groups proteins read without unwinding; 1bna is the B form found in cells, bent at the top by crystal packing, with propeller twisted bases; Watson and Crick in the 1950s; proteins repair DNA corrupted by chemicals or radiation.

motm-gfp.title: Molecule of the Month: Green Fluorescent Protein (GFP)
motm-gfp.checked: From a jellyfish in the cold north Pacific; turns blue light from aequorin into green light; absorbs ultraviolet and emits green; attached to proteins or viruses to watch them in cells; chromophore built from three amino acids (serine or threonine, tyrosine, glycine) buried inside; oxygen finishes the chromophore over about an hour; 1ema: the chain forms a cylindrical can with a strand through the middle and the chromophore in the centre, shielded from water.
motm-gfp.cite: Molecule of the Month: Green Fluorescent Protein (GFP)

motm-hemoglobin.title: Molecule of the Month: Hemoglobin
motm-hemoglobin.checked: Four chains, two alpha and two beta, each with a heme holding an iron atom; oxygen binds reversibly to the iron; first oxygen is hard to add, then binding gets easier; oxygen pulls a histidine under the heme; carbon monoxide replaces oxygen at the heme; sickle cell is glutamate 6 to valine in the beta chain, deoxy hemoglobin sticks into stiff fibers, cells become C or sickle shaped; Max Perutz solved horse hemoglobin (2dhb); 2hhb has no oxygen bound.

motm-insulin.title: Molecule of the Month: Insulin
motm-insulin.checked: Made in the pancreas, released after meals; tells liver, muscle and fat cells to take glucose out of the blood; made as a longer chain then clipped to two chains; three disulfide bridges; pig insulin (4ins) differs from human by one amino acid, alanine in place of threonine at the end of the chain; impaired insulin leads to diabetes mellitus; hexamer stores the hormone before release; hydrophobic core of leucine and isoleucine.

motm-lysozyme.title: Molecule of the Month: Lysozyme
motm-lysozyme.checked: Small enzyme that breaks the carbohydrate chains of bacterial cell walls so bacteria burst; Alexander Fleming discovered it when a drop of mucus killed bacteria; found in hen egg white, tears and mucus; first enzyme to have its structure solved (2lyz); long active site cleft binds the cell wall carbohydrate chain.

motm-myosin.title: Molecule of the Month: Myosin
motm-myosin.checked: Powers every voluntary and involuntary movement; captures and breaks ATP to make a power stroke; two heavy chains and four light chains; 1b7t contains only part of the molecule, the tail was clipped off, but includes most of the motor domain; about 300 myosins form a thick filament; heads climb actin filaments; release of phosphate powers the stroke, amplified by the lever arm; about 2 trillion myosins to hold up a baseball.

text.t: This heme is the oxygen seat of {chain}: one oxygen molecule binds to the iron atom at its centre.
With one heme in each of its four chains, one hemoglobin carries up to four oxygen molecules, picked up in the lungs and dropped off in the tissues.
Histidine 87 reaches up from below the heme and bonds to its iron.
When oxygen lands on the iron it pulls this histidine, and the shift spreads to the other chains so they grab oxygen more easily.
In the beta chains, histidine 92 is the one that bonds to the heme iron from below.
When oxygen lands on the iron it pulls this histidine, and the shift spreads to the other chains so they grab oxygen more easily.
Histidine 58 sits in the pocket above the heme, at the spot where oxygen binds.
Histidine 63 is the beta chain's second heme histidine, on the far side of the heme from histidine 92.
Position 6 of each beta chain is glutamate in normal hemoglobin.
In sickle cell hemoglobin it is valine, and that one change lets the molecules stick together into stiff fibers.
This amino acid is one of the spots on the beta chain that hold 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (BPG), a small molecule that binds to hemoglobin.

holdsExtra.t: Its glowing chromophore is built from the chain's own amino acids, so it is drawn as part of the ribbon.

text.t: This is the chromophore, the part that absorbs light and glows green.
It forms by itself from three amino acids of the chain: serine 65, tyrosine 66 and glycine 67 in the jellyfish protein, with threonine at 65 in this version.
The glycine bonds to the serine to close a new ring, and over about an hour oxygen from the surroundings finishes the glowing group.
The can of protein around it shields it from water molecules that would otherwise steal its energy.
Threonine 203 sits next to the chromophore.
Changing it to tyrosine or histidine shifts the light toward red, one way scientists made new colours.
The chain runs straight into the chromophore here: it is joined to phenylalanine 64 on one side and valine 68 on the other.
This stretch is the central helix that runs through the middle of the can.
This is one of the two NPA loops (asparagine, proline, alanine) that dip into the membrane, the signature of every aquaporin.
Their two asparagines hold the central water in a fixed direction, so the channel cannot pass protons along a chain of water.
Histidine 182 lines the tightest part of the pore, the long, narrow filter that decides what gets through.
It is found in every known water-only channel and helps make sure that only water gets through.
This part of the chain is one of six helices that cross the membrane, the frame that holds the water pore.
Water molecules pass through the pore one at a time, in single file.
Glutamate 35 is one of the enzyme's two active-site amino acids, with aspartate 52.
Together they cut the sugar chain of a bacterial cell wall in the long cleft, and the bacterium then bursts under its own pressure.
Aspartate 52 is one of the enzyme's two active-site amino acids, with glutamate 35.
Together they cut the sugar chain of a bacterial cell wall in the long cleft, and the bacterium then bursts under its own pressure.
This cysteine is half of one of four disulfide bridges that staple the chain to itself in this small, stable enzyme.
Amino acids 75 to 80 (threonine, valine, glycine, tyrosine, glycine, aspartate: TVGYGD) form the selectivity filter, where the four chains meet around the pore.
The filter lets potassium ions through but blocks sodium: only one sodium ion passes for every ten thousand potassium ions.
This short helix sits inside the membrane and helps form the pore, just below the filter.
One of the three potassium ions this crystal caught inside the pore.
Nerve cells rely on channels like this one: potassium flows out through them to reset the cell after a signal.
This loop of the beta subunit holds the phosphates of ADP, ATP and free phosphate.
The beta subunits are the catalytic ones, where ADP and phosphate are joined into ATP.
Glutamate 188 helps hold the magnesium ion that sits with the nucleotide in this catalytic site.
This ADP sits in a catalytic site of the beta subunit, one of the two pieces that get joined into ATP.
This ATP sits in the alpha subunit, the partner that forms the catalytic core with beta but does not make ATP itself.
The gamma subunit is the axle in the middle of the head.
As the axle turns, its odd shape forces the surrounding subunits through the steps of making ATP.
Serine 200 does the cutting: it bonds to the acetyl group of acetylcholine and breaks the molecule.
A water molecule then frees the serine, ready for the next acetylcholine.
Part of the serine, histidine, glutamate trio at the bottom of the active-site pocket, helping serine 200 break acetylcholine.
Tacrine, a drug, sits in the deep active-site gorge.
Some drugs for Alzheimer's disease work by partly blocking this enzyme.
Aspartate 25 of each chain meets its twin at the centre of the tunnel, and these two aspartates do all of the cutting.
Ritonavir sits in the tunnel where a protein chain would be cut.
The enzyme cannot cut it, so it stays lodged in the active site and blocks the enzyme.
Lysine 201 carries an extra carbon dioxide, which acts as an activator, and helps hold the magnesium ion in the active site.
Aspartate 203 and glutamate 204 help hold the magnesium ion at the centre of the active site.
One of the two active-site amino acids (lysine 175 and histidine 294) that take up a proton during the carbon-fixing reaction.
Rubisco's active site is centred on this magnesium ion.
When the enzyme is active, the free side of the magnesium binds the sugar so it can react with carbon dioxide.
Lysine 296 forms a covalent bond with retinal, holding it deep inside the protein.
That bond makes sure the light-driven change in retinal's shape is passed on to the protein around it.
Retinal is the part that catches light: when it absorbs a photon, one bond flips from a bent to an extended shape.
Opsin holds it in a strained shape, which makes the flip happen about twice as often as in free retinal.
Glutamate 113 plays an important part in the switch to the active shape.
Glutamate, arginine and tyrosine here form the 'ionic lock', which helps steady the activated form.
Cysteines 110 and 187 are joined by a disulfide bridge.
This heme is where myoglobin stores oxygen: the iron in its centre holds one oxygen molecule.
The heme sits in a deep pocket on one side of the protein.
Histidine 93 holds the heme iron from the side away from the oxygen.
Histidine 64 sits at the spot where oxygen binds to the heme iron.
Aspartate 32 and aspartate 215 are pepsin's two active-site aspartates.
They activate a water molecule and use it to cut protein chains in the deep groove.
This amino acid lines the groove at the top of the heavy chain and helps grip the peptide on display.
MHC holds short pieces of the cell's proteins like this one so the immune system can check them, and a cell showing viral pieces is killed.
The file models this peptide as a chain of 9 amino acids.
This cysteine is part of one of three disulfide bridges that hold insulin together: one inside the A chain and two joining A to B.
This cysteine forms one of the two disulfide bridges that join the B chain to the A chain.
In this crystal, histidine 10 of the B chain grips a zinc ion.
Six insulins gather around two zinc ions to form a hexamer, the form used to store the hormone before release.
This is pig insulin, and it differs from human insulin only here: alanine at the end of the B chain where humans have threonine.
One of the two zinc ions in this crystal, held by histidine 10 of the B chains.
Six insulins gather around two zinc ions to form a hexamer, the form used to store the hormone before release.
Here the researchers put a bigger alanine where a glycine should be.
It crowds the neighbouring chains and makes the helix untwist a little at this spot.
Every third amino acid is glycine, small enough to tuck into the crowded centre of the triple helix.
Hydroxyproline is proline with an extra oxygen added after the chain is built, a step that needs vitamin C.
In this crystal, hydroxyprolines help hold a sleeve of water molecules around the helix.
Proline and hydroxyproline bend each chain smoothly around the helix.
This ADP sits deep in the groove between actin's two arms.
Actin carries ATP when it joins a filament, then splits it to ADP, and ADP-actin lets go more easily.
Small calcium ions are bound around the protein, and one of them holds onto a phosphate of the ADP.
Myosin catches ATP here and splits it into ADP and phosphate.
This crystal caught it holding ADP and a magnesium ion.
A magnesium ion sits with the ADP in the fuel site.
The heavy chain holds most of the motor domain, the part that makes the power stroke.
Two small light chains ride along with the heavy chain: chain Y is the regulatory light chain and chain Z the essential light chain.

1.name: Kinesin heavy chain, motor head piece

text.t: Each of the two motor heads holds an ADP.
Kinesin is one of the cell's ATP-powered motors, crawling hand over hand along microtubules.
This adenine pairs with a thymine on the other strand.
The A and T pairs in the middle of this piece are propeller twisted, not perfectly flat, which helps the bases stack.
This thymine pairs with an adenine on the other strand.
This guanine pairs with a cytosine on the other strand, held by hydrogen bonds across the middle of the helix.
This cytosine pairs with a guanine on the other strand, held by hydrogen bonds across the middle of the helix.
This histone is one of eight bundled tightly together, with the DNA wrapped around them in two loops.
One strand of the 146 base pair DNA wrapped around the histone spool, a sequence taken from the human X chromosome.
Nucleosomes protect the delicate DNA strands in our cells from physical damage.
